summary: For ages 10–11: multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 (answers up to three decimal places, with 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 as a four-decimal-place extension) by understanding that every DIGIT shifts position across the place-value chart while the decimal point stays fixed at the ones boundary. The organising principle is 'digits move, the point stays'; ×10 shifts each digit one column left (each digit becomes ten times bigger), ÷10 shifts one column right, and the number of places matches the number of zeros in the power of ten. Placeholder zeros fill vacated columns (e.g. 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452). This counters the 'just add a zero' habit, which breaks for decimals, and gives a place-value reason for 'move the point', which gets correct answers but is often learned without understanding.
misconceptions: 'Add a zero when you multiply by 10' — wrong for decimals (2.5 × 10 ≠ 2.50) and a source of place-value damage.
'Move the decimal point' — leads to moving the point the wrong way or mispositioning it; the point is fixed, the digits move.
Omitting placeholder zeros when dividing (45.2 ÷ 1000 written as 0.452 or .0452 rather than 0.0452).
Confusing the DIRECTION: multiplying making the number smaller (shifting right) or dividing making it larger.
Shifting only one digit or the wrong number of places, especially for ×/÷1000 (three places).

activities.title: Slide the digits across a place-value chart
steps: Set up a place-value chart with columns from thousands down to ten-thousandths, with the decimal point marked fixed at the ones boundary (ThHTO . tenths hundredths thousandths ten-thousandths); the extra low columns are needed because 45.2 ÷ 1000 lands a digit in the ten-thousandths place.
Write 3.456 into the chart using digit cards, then multiply by 100: slide EVERY digit two columns to the LEFT in one move, keeping the point pinned in place, to land on 345.6.

Now take 45.2 and divide by 1000: slide every digit three columns to the RIGHT (the tenths digit travels into the ten-thousandths column), and write a placeholder 0 into each emptied column that is written (ones and tenths) to get 0.0452.
Say aloud for each step: 'the digits moved ___ places ___ because I multiplied/divided by ___', linking the number of places to the power of ten.
Try a target challenge: starting from 3.456, work out which single operation reaches 345.6, and which reaches 0.3456.
activities.insight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten moves every digit a fixed number of place-value columns while the decimal point stays put; the number of columns equals the number of zeros in the power of ten, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.

activities.title: Why ten-times moves each digit one column
steps: Pick a digit in a number, e.g. the 4 in 3.456 (worth four tenths), and state its value.
Explain why, when the whole number is made ten times bigger, that digit must now be worth ten times as much (four ones) and therefore move one column to the left.
Use a scaling chart or a 'ten-times' number line to show the whole quantity becoming ten times as large, not merely gaining an extra written digit.
Chain the reasoning: ×100 is ×10 then ×10, so each digit moves one column left twice — two columns in total — and connect ÷10 as the exact inverse (one column right).
activities.insight: Because each place-value column is worth ten times the column to its right, making a number ten times bigger promotes every digit into the next-higher column; this is WHY the shift happens and why ×100 shifts two columns and ÷1000 three.

activities.title: Fluency and error checks
steps: Complete fill-in-the-blank items such as 45.2 ÷ 1000 = ____ , writing all placeholder zeros, and 3.456 × 100 = ____ .
Answer direction questions: when dividing by a power of ten, which way do the digits move, and how many places for ÷1000?
Order a set of results by size, e.g. 2.5 × 10, 2.5 × 100, 2.5 × 1000, and explain the ordering by place-value shift.
Self-check each answer by counting the columns crossed against the number of zeros in the multiplier or divisor.
activities.insight: Repeated practice with answers up to three decimal places (plus the four-decimal-place extension 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452) is intended to make the power-of-ten ↔ number-of-places mapping more automatic and to surface the common errors (missing placeholder zeros, wrong direction, miscounting by one).

activities.title: Challenge the 'add a zero' habit through dialogue
steps: Consider a claim a friend might make: '2.5 × 10 = 2.50'. Explain exactly what has gone wrong and give the correct answer with reasoning.
Explain why 3.456 × 100 is not 3.45600, referring to where each digit sits in the place-value chart.
Describe, in your own words, when 'add a zero' happens to look right (whole numbers) and why it fails for decimals.
activities.insight: The 'add a zero' rule is unreliable for decimals because it ignores place value. 'Move the point' gives correct answers, but used as a bare rule it hides why. Explaining the flaw is intended to strengthen the digits-move model.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to work these while you watch, using a place-value chart if they like: 3.456 × 100, then 45.2 ÷ 1000. Watch whether they SHIFT each digit the right number of places (with the point staying put) or fall back on 'add/remove zeros' and 'move the point', and whether they insert placeholder zeros.
checkAnswer: 345.6; 0.0452. The teacher watches for each digit shifting two places left (×100) and three places right (÷1000), the decimal point staying fixed while digits move, and placeholder zeros inserted (the leading 0.0452).
